name: Help Scout
tagline: An email-first shared inbox built to never look like a ticketing system, with a source-restricted AI agent billed at $0.75 a resolution.
tldr: Help Scout is a shared-inbox help desk built around email, a live chat widget (Beacon), and a hosted knowledge base (Docs) — deliberately designed so customers never see ticket numbers or a portal, with AI layered on afterwards rather than built in from the start.

Pricing is per user per month — Free ($0), Standard ($25), Plus ($45), Pro ($75), roughly 16% off annually — plus the AI Answers chatbot as a separate usage charge at $0.75 per resolution, and $10/mo per extra inbox, $20/mo per extra Docs site (helpscout.com/pricing).

The differentiator is restraint: it's the least ticket-shaped help desk in this category, and the review evidence backs that up — 4.6/5 across 226 Capterra reviews and 4.4/5 across ~435 G2 reviews, with 'intuitive' and 'minimal training needed' as the recurring themes.

Real strength: every paid plan includes generous free light users (15 on Standard, 25 on Plus, 50 on Pro) for people who only need to read and comment — a meaningful cost saver versus per-seat rivals.

Real weakness: the late-2024 pivot to contact-based billing and its subsequent partial reversal left a dual pricing system and a documented trail of large increases for existing customers, including a Trustpilot reviewer reporting a jump from $1,500/yr to over $7,500/yr.

Best for small-to-mid support teams whose volume is mostly email and whose priority is a fast, human-feeling inbox — not for teams needing native voice, agentic AI that can take actions, or deep custom reporting.
keyFeatures: Shared inbox where email, Beacon live chat, and connected Meta/WhatsApp channels land in one conversation thread per customer, with no customer-facing ticket numbers or portal
Docs — a hosted, customer-facing knowledge base that doubles as the training source for AI Answers (1 site on Free, up to 5 on Pro, $20/mo per additional site)
AI Answers: an autonomous self-service agent embedded in Beacon, restricted to your knowledge base and specified web/document sources, billed at $0.75 per resolution
Inbox Assistant for agents — AI Drafts (one-click reply generation trained on your docs plus your team's past replies), AI Summarize for long threads, and AI Assist for tone, grammar, and translation
Workflows and SLA policies for routing, tagging, and escalation — 150 basic workflows on Free, 500 advanced on Standard, unlimited on Plus and Pro
Light users included free on every plan (15 Standard / 25 Plus / 50 Pro) for stakeholders who need read and comment access without a full seat
Customer profiles with company-level context, prior conversation history, and sidebar data pulled from connected apps like Shopify, HubSpot, and Salesforce
Mailbox API v2, Docs API, Beacon JavaScript API, and webhooks with published rate limits (200 requests/min per account; 12 writes per 5 seconds)

companyInfo.founded: 2011 — incorporated April 17, 2011 by Nick Francis, Jared McDaniel, and Denny Swindle as a pivot from design consultancy Brightwurks, launched via Techstars Boston
companyInfo.hq: Boston, Massachusetts, USA — fully distributed team; Help Scout's own about page says its remote team works from over 115 cities
companyInfo.funding: Approximately $14.1M raised across six rounds per Tracxn (seed rounds of $435K in 2011 and $704K in 2012, a $6M Series A in March 2015); incorporated as a public benefit corporation (Help Scout PBC) and a Pledge 1% signatory
companyInfo.employees: Not officially disclosed. Wikipedia cites roughly 100 employees across 80+ cities; third-party tracker LeadIQ lists ~292 as of April 2026. Treat the exact headcount as unverified — Help Scout's own site gives city count, not headcount.

faq.question: Is Help Scout priced per seat or per contact?
faq.answer: Per seat, as of the current public pricing page — Free, Standard at $25/user/mo, Plus at $45, Pro at $75. Help Scout switched to contact-based billing around November 2024 and then brought per-user pricing back as the default for new signups after significant customer pushback. The practical consequence is a dual system: what you'd sign up for today is not necessarily what a long-tenured customer is paying, and Help Scout's own legacy-plan documentation confirms older plans exist and can be migrated with six months' notice.

faq.question: How does Help Scout charge for AI?
faq.answer: Two different ways. The agent-side Inbox Assistant (AI Drafts, AI Summarize, AI Assist) is bundled into Standard and above at no extra usage cost. The customer-facing AI Answers chatbot is billed separately at $0.75 per resolution, in arrears. Help Scout defines a resolution as a single AI chat session closed without human help — you're charged once per session no matter how many questions the AI answered, and not charged at all if the AI only greeted the customer or asked a follow-up without giving a full answer. Account owners can set a monthly resolution spending cap that disables AI Answers when hit. New customers get a three-month free trial of AI Answers; existing customers do not.

faq.question: Can Help Scout's AI look up a customer's order status?
faq.answer: Not that Help Scout documents. AI Answers is explicitly scoped to your Docs knowledge base, specified websites or subdomains, and publicly accessible documents — Help Scout states its answers "will only ever use the sources you provide." Order data does reach the human agent's sidebar via the Shopify integration (which supports viewing order status and issuing refunds inside Help Scout), but there is no documented tool-calling or action-execution capability that would let the AI agent itself query a live order record.

faq.question: Does Help Scout support phone or voice support?
faq.answer: Not natively. Help Scout's feature marketing references phone as a supported channel, but the connectable-channels documentation lists only Email (all plans) plus Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp (paid plans). Voice in practice means a third-party integration such as Aircall or Talkdesk, and the Pro plan advertises preferred Aircall pricing — which is itself a tell that the telephony is someone else's product.

faq.question: What is Help Scout's claimed AI resolution rate, and should I trust it?
faq.answer: Help Scout's AI features page states companies average a 73.19% resolution rate with AI Answers. Read the definition before the number: resolutions are counted when the customer doesn't escalate, doesn't search the knowledge base, and doesn't indicate they need more help after a response. That measures the absence of a visible complaint, not verified correctness — a customer who gives up and leaves counts as resolved. No independent benchmark corroborating the figure was found.

faq.question: How does Help Scout compare to Zendesk for a small team?
faq.answer: Cheaper and materially simpler, at the cost of depth. Standard at $25/user/mo undercuts Zendesk's Suite Team at $55/agent/mo, and Help Scout's whole design premise is that the customer never encounters a ticketing interface. But Zendesk gives you native telephony, deeper routing, and far more configurable reporting — and Help Scout reviewers on both G2 and Capterra consistently name reporting as the weak spot, with advanced reports gated to higher tiers.

criteriaScores.note: Email, Beacon live chat, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger are supported, with the pricing page also listing SMS under Standard — though Help Scout's own connectable-channels documentation enumerates only Email, Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp, so SMS's status as a first-party channel is not cleanly verifiable. No native voice/telephony: phone means Aircall or Talkdesk (helpscout.com/pricing, docs.helpscout.com article 1510).

Connected channels genuinely land in the same Inbox and inherit the same tags, workflows, and assignment rules rather than sitting in separate per-channel views, per Help Scout's channel documentation and WhatsApp integration page. Held back from a 5 only because voice never enters that view at all.

AI Answers is a real autonomous customer-facing agent embedded in Beacon — configurable sources, its own resolution reporting, and its own per-resolution billing line — alongside a separate agent-side Inbox Assistant. This is more than canned smart replies, though it arrived as a layer on a fourteen-year-old inbox rather than as the core architecture (helpscout.com/ai-features).

Help Scout advertises a 73.19% average resolution rate, but its own definition counts a resolution whenever the customer doesn't escalate, search the knowledge base, or ask for more help — a non-escalation proxy that scores an abandoned chat as a success. No independent benchmark corroborating the figure was found, and G2/Capterra sentiment about the AI is thin enough that it offers no counterweight either way (helpscout.com/ai-features, docs.helpscout.com article 1746).

No manual intent-building required: agents are pointed at a Help Scout Docs knowledge base, a website or specific subdomain, and publicly accessible PDFs/spreadsheets. AI Drafts additionally learns from replies your team has already written, which is the more useful of the two training paths (helpscout.com/blog/help-scout-ai-features).

Help Scout states answers "will only ever use the sources you provide — never content from the general web," transcripts expose which sources the agent consulted so teams can find knowledge gaps, and the bot is explicitly labeled as AI rather than passed off as human. What's missing is customer-facing per-answer source citation or a tunable confidence threshold — the retrieval is fenced, but the customer can't check its work (helpscout.com/ai-features).

Workflows are condition/action rules — plan-metered at 150 basic on Free, 500 advanced on Standard, unlimited on Plus/Pro — plus SLA policies and round-robin routing. That covers routing, tagging, and escalation, but there is no documented agentic capability: the AI resolves by answering from documents, not by chaining steps or executing actions in connected systems.

No sentiment or intent detection feature appears anywhere in Help Scout's own AI features page, AI blog post, or AI support documentation, all of which enumerate the AI capabilities exhaustively (AI Answers, AI Drafts, AI Summarize, AI Assist). Frustration flagging and urgency detection appear to simply not exist as a product feature — scored on documented absence, not on a failed capability.

This is the entire product, and it's the thing reviewers actually praise: one thread per customer, company-level context, prior conversation history, and connected-app data all in a single pane, with no customer-facing ticket UI. Capterra's 4.6/5 across 226 reviews is driven overwhelmingly by exactly this (helpscout.com/features, capterra.com/p/136909/Help-Scout/reviews).

Help Scout documents that human help is "just two clicks away" from an AI Answers session, lets you customize the transfer text shown when the agent hands off to live chat, and — notably — doesn't bill the $0.75 resolution fee when the customer escalates, which aligns the vendor's incentive with a clean handoff (helpscout.com/ai-features, docs.helpscout.com article 1746).

Internal notes, manual or automatic conversation assignment, custom filtered views (e.g. VIP, waiting over 24 hours), and AI Summarize for bringing a teammate up to speed on a long thread are all documented native features. Capterra reviewer Fernando L. specifically credits ticket assignment and internal note sharing with streamlining team communication (helpscout.com/features).

Saved Replies are a first-class feature across all plans, though the Free tier caps them at 10 (alongside 10 tags). Straightforward and unremarkable in the good way (helpscout.com/pricing, helpscout.com/features).

First-party integration in Help Scout's own directory, described as "View order status, give refunds, and more, all inside Help Scout" — write actions, not just a read-only sidebar. The limitation is that this serves the human agent; the AI agent has no documented access to it (helpscout.com/help-desk-integration/shopify).

A WooCommerce integration exists but is built and sold by a third party (OPMC) at $8.25, not by Help Scout. It surfaces lifetime value, average order value, and up to 10 recent orders in the customer profile pane — read-only context, with no refund or write actions comparable to the Shopify app (helpscout.com/help-desk-integration/woocommerce).

The Help Scout plugin on WordPress.org is authored by BoldGrid with Help Scout listed only as a contributor, and has ~400+ active installs — a thin footprint. It embeds the Beacon widget and adds a contact form that posts to Help Scout (contact form requires a paid plan for API access). Functionally this is a script embed, not a WordPress-native product surface (wordpress.org/plugins/help-scout).

Help Scout documents Wix installation in its own support docs (article 1348), but the method is pasting the Beacon embed code — no Wix App Market app was found. It works; it just isn't an integration in any meaningful sense beyond a script tag.

Same pattern as Wix: an official Help Scout doc (article 1347) instructing you to paste the Beacon embed into Settings > Advanced > Code Injection in the header field. Documented and reliable, but manual code injection rather than a native app.

Documented in Help Scout's support docs (article 1440), but installation requires adding an Embed element in the Webflow designer and pasting Beacon code — and Help Scout's own doc notes this depends on your Webflow plan including the Embed option, which adds a plan-level dependency on top of the manual step.

Zapier and Make both appear in Help Scout's official integration directory, and Help Scout's own copy positions Zapier as the route to "50+ more apps." No n8n listing was found in the first-party directory. Adequate coverage of the mainstream no-code platforms, without the three-way breadth some rivals offer (helpscout.com/help-desk-integration).

HubSpot (contacts and deal pipelines in the conversation sidebar) and Salesforce (CRM records and customer activity in the sidebar) are both first-party integrations — but the pricing page gates Salesforce, Jira, and HubSpot to Plus and above, so a $25/user Standard customer doesn't get them. No Pipedrive integration was found in the first-party directory (helpscout.com/help-desk-integration, helpscout.com/pricing).

The human agent can see order status and issue refunds via the Shopify sidebar, so the data reaches the inbox. The bot cannot: AI Answers is documented as answering only from your knowledge base, specified websites, and uploaded documents, with no tool-calling or live data-lookup capability described anywhere in Help Scout's AI documentation. For a WISMO-heavy ecommerce workload, that's the AI doing none of the actual work.

Help Scout states AI Answers operates across 50+ languages, and AI Assist includes translation for agent replies. What isn't documented is automatic detection of and response in the customer's language as a configurable behavior — the language capability is confirmed, the auto-detection workflow is not (helpscout.com/ai-features).

Covers the fundamentals — conversation volume, response and resolution times, Happiness (CSAT) reports, agent and team performance, per-channel breakdowns, filtering by inbox/tag/folder/custom field, CSV and Excel export, plus AI resolution and escalation reporting. But reporting history is capped (30 days Free, 2 years Standard, all-time only on Plus/Pro), and it's the single most consistent complaint in independent reviews: one G2 reviewer writes that "some advanced features and reporting options are limited unless you move to higher plans," and a Capterra reviewer that "the reporting isn't as advanced as some tools out there."

The current model is unusually well documented — public per-user tiers, a published $0.75/resolution AI price with an explicit definition of what does and doesn't count, and configurable monthly spend caps. What costs it points is history and structure: the November 2024 pivot to contact-based billing and the subsequent quiet return to per-user pricing left legacy plans running in parallel, and Help Scout's own legacy-plan doc promises six months' notice of increases rather than protection from them (helpscout.com/pricing, docs.helpscout.com articles 1300 and 1746).

Mailbox API v2, Docs API v1, a Beacon JavaScript API for widget customization, webhooks for real-time event notifications, and open-source tooling, with rate limits published openly (200 requests/minute per account; an additional 12 write requests per 5 seconds, returning 429 with Retry-After). Genuine build-on-top capability rather than a closed workflow builder (developer.helpscout.com).

pricing.model: Per-user tiered SaaS, plus separate usage-based billing for the customer-facing AI agent and metered add-ons for extra inboxes and knowledge-base sites

plans.name: Free
plans.notes: 1 inbox, 1 Docs site, 100 contacts/month, 5 light users, 10 saved replies, 10 tags, 150 basic workflows, 1 basic SLA policy, 30-day reporting history

plans.name: Standard
plans.notes: 2 inboxes, 2 Docs sites, unlimited contacts, 15 light users, live chat and SMS, WhatsApp/Instagram/Messenger, 500 advanced workflows, 2-year reporting history, AI Inbox Assistant (Drafts, Summarize, Assist)

plans.name: Plus
plans.notes: 5 inboxes, 3 Docs sites, 25 light users, unlimited advanced workflows and SLA policies, customer portal, round-robin routing, all-time reporting history, Salesforce/Jira/HubSpot integrations

plans.name: Pro
plans.notes: 10 inboxes, 5 Docs sites, 50 light users, multiple routing types, SSO/SAML, HIPAA compliance, dedicated onboarding and a strategic account manager, preferred Aircall pricing

plans.name: AI Answers (add-on)
plans.notes: Available on Standard and above. A resolution is one AI chat session closed without human help; greetings and follow-up questions without a full answer aren't billed, and escalated sessions aren't billed. 3-month free trial for customers new to Help Scout only. Monthly spend caps configurable by the account owner.

plans.name: Add-ons
plans.billing: Annual pricing ($12 and $24 respectively on monthly billing)
plans.notes: Charged beyond the counts included in your plan

pricingBreakdown: The headline number to actually reason about is $25/user/mo on Standard, and for a five-agent team that's $125/mo — comfortably under Intercom's Essential at $29/seat ($145/mo) and less than half Zendesk's Suite Team at $55/agent ($275/mo). Where Help Scout quietly wins is the light-user allowance: 15 free on Standard, 25 on Plus, 50 on Pro, for people who need to read and comment but not work the queue. Intercom only starts handing out Lite seats at Advanced ($85/seat), so a company with a handful of agents and a long tail of curious stakeholders genuinely pays less here. On AI, $0.75 per resolution undercuts Intercom's Fin at $0.99 — but note that Help Scout's resolution definition (customer didn't escalate, didn't search the knowledge base, didn't ask for more help) is generous to the vendor in a way that makes the per-unit comparison less clean than it looks; you may simply be billed for more units. Compared to Crisp's flat $95/mo Essentials covering 10 seats, Help Scout is straightforwardly more expensive per head and always will be — per-user pricing is per-user pricing. The real cost risk isn't the sticker price at all, though; it's the billing model itself changing underneath you. Help Scout moved to contact-based pricing in late 2024, moved back, and left legacy plans running in parallel — with a documented policy of six months' notice before a price increase, which is a notification guarantee, not a price guarantee.

capabilities.note: This is the actual product and everything else is an accessory to it. Email, Beacon chat, and connected Meta/WhatsApp conversations land in one thread per customer with company-level context, prior history, and sidebar app data. The design constraint that makes it distinctive is what's absent: no customer-facing ticket numbers, no portal, no reference IDs in the subject line. Reviewers on Capterra and G2 name intuitiveness as the top strength with near-total consistency, and that isn't accidental — it's the one thing this company has spent fourteen years optimizing.

Docs is a real, standalone hosted help center, not a bolt-on — 1 site on Free scaling to 5 on Pro, at $20/mo for each one beyond your allowance. Its strategic role has changed, though: since AI Answers trains on it, Docs is now the input that determines whether your AI agent is any good. If your documentation is thin, AI Answers will be too, and no amount of tuning will fix that because there's nothing else it's allowed to read.

A genuine self-service agent in the Beacon widget, fenced to your own sources with no general-web content, labeled as AI rather than disguised as a person, and priced per resolution with a spending cap you control. It's an honest implementation of a narrow idea. What it is not is agentic: it answers questions from documents and it escalates. It cannot look up an order, process a return, or execute anything in a connected system, and nothing in Help Scout's documentation suggests otherwise.

The part of the AI story that's actually included in your seat price and, in my read, the more useful half. AI Drafts generates a reply from your docs plus your team's own past replies — that second source matters, because it's what makes drafts sound like your team rather than like a manual. AI Summarize condenses long threads for handoffs, and AI Assist handles tone, grammar, and translation. Unglamorous, bundled, no per-use meter.

Condition-and-action rules for assignment, tagging, escalation, and SLA enforcement, metered by plan — 150 basic on Free, 500 advanced on Standard, unlimited on Plus and Pro, with round-robin arriving at Plus and additional routing types at Pro. Perfectly competent for a mid-sized queue. It is rules automation, not orchestration, and there's no bridge between the AI agent and the workflow engine that would let the bot trigger multi-step processes.

The weakest area and the one independent reviewers flag most often. You get volume, response and resolution times, Happiness/CSAT, per-agent and per-team performance, channel breakdowns, filtering, CSV/Excel export, and AI resolution reporting — the fundamentals are all present. What's constrained is history and depth: 30 days on Free, 2 years on Standard, all-time only from Plus. If reporting is how you run your support org rather than how you report on it, budget for Plus at minimum and still expect to export to a spreadsheet.

pros: Genuinely the most intuitive inbox in this category, and the review data supports it rather than just the marketing — 4.6/5 across 226 Capterra reviews and 4.4/5 across ~435 G2 reviews, with low training overhead as the recurring theme
The no-ticket-interface design philosophy is a real product decision with real customer-experience consequences, not a positioning line — customers get replies that look like email, because they are
Free light users on every plan (15/25/50 on Standard/Plus/Pro) meaningfully undercut per-seat rivals for teams with many read-only stakeholders
AI pricing is unusually well specified: $0.75 per resolution with a published definition of what counts, no charge when the customer escalates, and an owner-configurable monthly spend cap
Solid developer surface — Mailbox API v2, Docs API, Beacon JS API, webhooks, and openly published rate limits (200 req/min; 12 writes per 5s) rather than a locked workflow builder
cons: Pricing-model instability is the standout risk: contact-based billing arrived in late 2024, was walked back to per-user as the default, and left legacy plans running in parallel — with one Trustpilot reviewer documenting an increase from $1,500/yr to over $7,500/yr

The AI can't do anything but answer — no tool calling, no order lookups, no actions in connected systems — which makes it a poor fit for transactional ecommerce support no matter how good your docs are
Reporting is the most consistently criticized area across G2 and Capterra, with all-time history and advanced reports gated to Plus ($45/user) and above
No native voice channel; phone support means Aircall or Talkdesk, and no sentiment or intent detection appears anywhere in Help Scout's own AI documentation

Several website-builder 'integrations' (Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, WordPress) are documented copy-paste embed instructions rather than first-party apps — the WordPress plugin isn't even authored by Help Scout

sentiment.quote: The Help Scout platform is one of the most user-friendly interfaces I have encountered.
They just announced they are 'upgrading' our plan from 1500 a year to over 7500 a year.
The reporting isn't as advanced as some tools out there.

bestFor: Small-to-mid support teams whose volume is predominantly email and who want conversations to feel like conversations rather than tickets
Companies with a documentation habit already — Docs quality directly determines AI Answers quality, so teams that write things down get disproportionate value
Organizations with a small agent core and a large ring of read-only stakeholders, where the free light-user allowance materially changes the bill
Teams migrating off Zendesk who found the ticketing interface heavier than their actual support workload justified
verdict: Help Scout is what I'd recommend to a team that wants support software to feel like email and never make the customer say the word 'ticket.' Fourteen years of building essentially one thing shows: 4.6/5 across 226 Capterra reviews, 4.4/5 across roughly 435 on G2, and the praise is always the same specific praise — it's intuitive, new agents stop needing training. That's rarer than vendors make it sound. What I can't recommend without a warning is the pricing relationship. Help Scout tore up per-seat billing for contact-based billing in late 2024, absorbed the backlash, and quietly restored per-user pricing as the default for new signups — leaving existing customers stranded in between. One Trustpilot reviewer documented going from $1,500 a year to over $7,500. Help Scout's own docs promise six months' notice before a legacy plan increases, which is a policy about how you'll be told the price is going up, not that it won't. On AI, be realistic about what you're buying. AI Answers is an honest, source-fenced self-service agent at $0.75 a resolution, cheaper per unit than Fin's $0.99. But it answers from documents and nothing else. It can't look up an order, and the advertised 73.19% resolution rate counts any session where the customer didn't escalate — a non-escalation proxy dressed as accuracy, with no independent benchmark behind it. Buy Help Scout for the inbox, not the robot.
